svg.aria-label: Diagram: AWS Config now supports 10 additional resource types, and whether an account begins recording them is decided by its existing recording strategy rather than by any action taken today. An account configured to record all current and future resource types with exclusions picks up the ten automatically, adding configuration items and cost with no notification. An account that records a specific list of resource types picks up none of them, so its coverage gap grows by ten types while nothing appears to change. Neither outcome produces an event. The diagram also records what a non-recorded resource still provides: AWS Config captures only the creation and deletion of that resource and no other details at no cost, the details page shows null values for most configuration details and no relationship or configuration change information, and those create and delete notifications arrive during the periodic baselining process rather than when the resource was created or deleted. Finally it notes that coverage is the denominator of every compliance number, because a resource type Config does not record can be neither compliant nor non-compliant.
svg.title: Coverage is the denominator, and it just changed for some accounts and not others
svg.text: Ten new types. Your recording strategy decides whether you get them.
“AWS Config will automatically track these new additions” — if recording all types is on.
RECORD ALL CURRENT AND FUTURE
The ten start recording. No action, no notification.
New configuration items — and Config bills on them.
Coverage keeps pace with AWS; cost grows without
a decision being made.
RECORD A SPECIFIC LIST
Nothing happens. The list is explicit.
No new cost, and no new coverage.
The gap grew by ten types, and nothing in the
console will say so.
Neither outcome produces an event. In a mixed estate, coverage just diverged a little further.
What a non-recorded resource still gives you — better than nothing, worse than it looks
“AWS Config captures only the creation and deletion of that resource, and no other details, at no cost”
“null values for most configuration details … no information about relationships and configuration changes”
“create and delete notifications are not sent upon creation or deletion, but during the baselining process”
A console row with null configuration, arriving late. Reads as coverage in a screenshot.
Coverage is the denominator of every compliance number you report
A type Config does not record is not NON_COMPLIANT, and not COMPLIANT either. It is not counted.
A conformance pack rule for an unrecorded type returns nothing — which looks exactly like passing.
Find out which strategy each account actually uses.
In a large organisation it is rarely uniform, and the answer decides whether today was a cost event, a
coverage event, or nothing at all.
Exclusion is the strategy that ages well: new types arrive by default and you subtract the ones you do not
want. An inclusion list makes every AWS expansion a change request nobody raises.
Before reaching for daily recording to cut cost: “AWS Firewall Manager depends on continuous recording”.
